armour.title: Armour
armour.summary: Armour is rated by armour points, a skill penalty, and cost. Every blow is reduced by the armour points.
armour.summary_html: Armour is rated by armour points, a skill penalty, and cost. Every blow is reduced by the armour points.
armour.html:
Armour is worn for its armour points (AP), which reduce every blow that lands — see Working Out Damage. The trade-off is a skill penalty that applies while it is worn, and which also worsens a dodging defender's targeting difficulty. Heavier armour is also more expensive — see Weapons for what the same purse buys offensively.

Light armour

  • Partial leather — AP 1, skill penalty 0, cost 5gp.
  • Leather — AP 2, skill penalty -1, cost 10gp.
  • Studded leather — AP 3, skill penalty -2, cost 25gp.
  • Chain shirt — AP 4, skill penalty -3, cost 100gp.

Medium armour

  • Scale mail — AP 4, skill penalty -4, cost 50gp.
  • Chain mail — AP 5, skill penalty -4, cost 150gp.
  • Breastplate — AP 5, skill penalty -3, cost 200gp.
  • Full plate — AP 8, skill penalty -6, cost 1500gp.

attributes.title: Attributes
attributes.summary: Every character has six attributes — three physical, three mental — that describe their raw potential.
attributes.summary_html: Every character has six attributes — three physical, three mental — that describe their raw potential.
attributes.html:
A character's core potential is captured by 6 attributes. The physical ones are strength, dexterity and constitution; the mental ones are intelligence, willpower and charisma.

Reading a score

A score of 10 is average for a capable adult. Every 2 points above 10 gives a +1 bonus that applies to rolls governed by that attribute; every 2 points below gives a matching -1 penalty. A character's race can modify the raw scores before this bonus is worked out.

Which attribute governs which action is set by the skill in use — see Using and Focusing Skills — and attribute bonuses are one of the inputs to the core roll.

character-creation.title: Creating a Character
character-creation.summary: Spend a fixed pool of attribute points, choose skill focus, trade mastery hit points against skill points, take one power, and start with a set purse.
character-creation.summary_html: Spend a fixed pool of attribute points, choose skill focus, trade mastery hit points against skill points, take one power, and start with a set purse.
character-creation.html:
Build a starting character in this order.

Attributes

Split 80 points among the six Attributes. No score may start below 3 or above 18. Race modifiers apply after this spread, and the bonus for a high score is worked out from the final number.

Skill focus

Choose 1 skill group to be focused and 1 to be unfocused. Every other group is peripheral. What these tiers mean for how far a skill can be pushed is covered in Using and Focusing Skills.

Mastery hit points and skill points

Choose how many mastery hit points to start with, up to 15. Your starting skill points are 30 minus that number — every mastery hit point is a skill point you did not spend.

Powers and money

Take 1 power (see Using a Power) and 150 gold pieces to equip yourself from Weapons and Armour.

Priorities

Finally, apply your Setting Priorities — the trades that let one character start stronger in an area at the cost of being weaker, or more encumbered by circumstance, elsewhere.

core-resolution.title: The Core Roll
core-resolution.summary: Most actions are a d20 plus bonuses against either a fixed difficulty or an opposed roll. Beating the target by more means a better result.
core-resolution.summary_html: Most actions are a d20 plus bonuses against either a fixed difficulty or an opposed roll. Beating the target by more means a better result.
core-resolution.html:
When the outcome of an action is in doubt, you roll for it, and it is almost always the same roll.

The roll

Roll 1d20 and add your bonuses — from attributes, from the relevant skill, and from environmental factors the Dungeon Master calls out. Compare the total to a target, which is either:

  • a fixed difficulty set by the Dungeon Master, or
  • an opposed roll: someone else's 1d20

plus their own bonuses.

Meet or beat the target and you succeed.

Margin matters

Beating the target by more points is a better outcome, not just a success: more damage on a blow, less effort spent on a power, a faster or cleaner result. Individual rules say how their own margin is spent — see Landing a Blow and Working Out Damage for the combat case, and Using a Power for powers.

damage.title: Working Out Damage
damage.summary: Damage is the weapon's rating plus half the amount the attack beat the targeting difficulty, then reduced by armour and any block.
damage.summary_html: Damage is the weapon's rating plus half the amount the attack beat the targeting difficulty, then reduced by armour and any block.
damage.html:
Damage is only worked out once a blow has landed — see Landing a Blow.

The raw figure

Take the weapon's damage rating and add 0.5 times the amount by which the attack roll beat the targeting difficulty, rounding down. A weapon that beats a defence cleanly therefore does noticeably more than one that scrapes past it.

Reductions

The raw figure is then reduced:

  • by the armour rating of whatever the target is wearing, applied to

every blow — see Armour;

  • and, if the defender was blocking, by the armour points of the weapon

or shield used to block.

Applying it

Whatever is left comes off the target's hit points, taking mastery hit points first and reaching core hit points only once mastery is gone.

general-powers.title: General Powers
general-powers.summary: Powers any character may take, independent of specialisation. Each lists its source, its skill and its difficulty.
general-powers.summary_html: Powers any character may take, independent of specialisation. Each lists its source, its skill and its difficulty.
general-powers.html:
These powers are open to any character. Each is written as (power source, skill, difficulty), and is resolved as Using a Power describes. Powers tied to a particular specialisation are not covered here.

Fast Melee 1

(stamina, melee attack, difficulty 1)

Gain an extra melee attack, normally taken straight after your first.

Roll and modify the extra attack as normal and call the result R. First compare R to the power's difficulty to settle whether the power worked and what stamina it cost. If it worked, resolve the attack using that same R against the target's targeting difficulty.

Fast Melee 2

(stamina, melee attack, difficulty 6)

Gain a further extra melee attack. This can only be invoked directly after a Fast Melee 1 that cost no stamina. As before, the roll that tests the power is also the roll for the attack it grants.

Fast Melee 2 stacks with Fast Melee 1, and using the two together counts as a single power use.

Fast Ranged 1

(stamina, ranged attack, difficulty 1)

Gain an extra ranged attack. This works exactly like Fast Melee 1, but for ranged attacks.

hit-points.title: Core and Mastery Hit Points
hit-points.summary: Core hit points are your body and equal your constitution. Mastery hit points are luck and skill, and soak harm first.
hit-points.summary_html: Core hit points are your body and equal your constitution. Mastery hit points are luck and skill, and soak harm first.
hit-points.html:
Characters have two separate pools of hit points, and they mean different things.

Core hit points

Core hit points (CHP) are physical hardiness and the sheer will to keep going. A character's core hit points equal their constitution. Losing core hit points means real damage — a wound that actually landed.

Mastery hit points

Mastery hit points (MHP) are an accumulated cushion of luck, skill and experience. Losing mastery hit points is a near miss, a blow softened by rolling with it, a fight-ending strike that turned out to graze. They are bought as a character is built and advanced, traded against skill points — see Creating a Character.

Which pool takes the hit

Harm comes off mastery hit points first, and only reaches core hit points once mastery is exhausted. Working Out Damage covers how the size of a hit is worked out before it is applied here.

hitting.title: Landing a Blow
hitting.summary: The defender dodges or blocks, which sets the targeting difficulty. The attacker rolls d20 plus attack skill and must exceed it.
hitting.summary_html: The defender dodges or blocks, which sets the targeting difficulty. The attacker rolls d20 plus attack skill and must exceed it.
hitting.html:
Every blow is one attacker against one defender.

The defender chooses

Before the attack is rolled, the defender chooses to dodge or block, and that choice sets the targeting difficulty (TD) the attacker must beat.

  • Against a dodging defender, the TD is

10 plus the defender's dodge skill, before other modifiers. Most armour carries a dodge penalty, which lowers this number and makes a dodging wearer easier to hit.

  • Against a blocking defender, the TD is the defender's block skill,

usually modified by the block bonus or penalty of the weapon or shield being used.

The attacker rolls

The attacker rolls 1d20 plus their attack skill and applicable modifiers — see The Core Roll, and Using and Focusing Skills for which attack skill applies to which weapon. If the total is greater than the targeting difficulty, the blow lands and Working Out Damage is worked out. The amount by which the roll exceeds the TD is carried into that step, so a cleaner hit hurts more.

Weapon and shield block values used above are listed with the Weapons and Armour.

power-sources.title: Stamina and Spirit
power-sources.summary: Physical powers spend stamina, based on constitution. Magical powers spend spirit, based on will.
power-sources.summary_html: Physical powers spend stamina, based on constitution. Magical powers spend spirit, based on will.
power-sources.html:
There are two power sources, and every power draws on one of them.

  • Stamina fuels physical powers. Its base value is a character's

constitution.

  • Spirit fuels magical powers, spells included. Its base value is a

character's will.

Both can be raised by advancement, and possibly by items. Using a Power covers what a power costs from its source and how a good roll reduces that cost.

priorities.title: Setting Priorities
priorities.summary: A pool of priority points buys advantages at character creation, and can be topped up by taking matching disadvantages.
priorities.summary_html: A pool of priority points buys advantages at character creation, and can be topped up by taking matching disadvantages.
priorities.html:
Each character gets a number of priority points set by the Dungeon Master; the standard allowance is 4. Spend them on advantages, and take disadvantages to get more. This is done once, as part of Creating a Character.

Attributes

  • Spend 1 point for 4 extra

attribute points.

  • Gain 1 point by giving up

4 attribute points.

Skills

  • Spend 1 point for 5 extra skill

points, up to the normal skill maxima.

  • Spend 1 point to raise the maximum level of a single skill by one

step; this persists as the character advances.

  • Gain 1 point by giving up 5

skill points.

Powers

  • Spend 1 point for one extra power.
  • Gain 1 point by taking one fewer power.
  • Spend 1 point for a permanent

+3 bonus to one power source. This may only be taken once.

Wealth and circumstance

  • Spend 1 point for 500 extra

starting gold.

  • Spend 1 point for low-level connections;

spend two for high-level connections.

  • Spend two points to begin play landed.
  • Gain 1 point by starting with

100 less gold.

  • Gain 1 point by taking low-level enemies;

gain two by taking high-level enemies.

skill-list.title: The Skill List
skill-list.summary: Every skill and the attribute that governs it. Some governing attributes are not yet assigned.
skill-list.summary_html: Every skill and the attribute that governs it. Some governing attributes are not yet assigned.
skill-list.html:
Each entry is a skill and its governing attribute. Entries marked unassigned are carried over from an earlier draft and still need a governing attribute chosen; treat them as Dungeon-Master's-call for now. How high any of these can be raised depends on its focus tier — see Using and Focusing Skills.

Combat skills

  • Attack (melee) — strength. Used to hit with melee weapons.
  • Attack (ranged) — dexterity. Used to hit with ranged weapons, and

to place spells that need an attack roll.

  • Block — strength. Sets the targeting difficulty when blocking.
  • Dodge — dexterity. Sets the targeting difficulty when

dodging.

  • Fortitude — constitution. Resisting physical duress: poison,

disease, exhaustion.

  • Willpower — willpower. Resisting mental duress: fear, domination,

pain.

Magic

  • Spellcasting — intelligence or willpower. The single skill used to

cast every spell; see How Spellcasting Works.

  • Concentration — constitution.
  • Use magic device — unassigned.

General skills

  • Appraise — intelligence.
  • Balance — dexterity.
  • Bluff — charisma.
  • Climb — strength.
  • Craft — intelligence.
  • Decipher script — intelligence.
  • Diplomacy — charisma.
  • Disable device — intelligence.
  • Disguise — charisma.
  • Escape artist — dexterity.
  • Forgery — intelligence.
  • Gather information — unassigned.
  • Handle animal — unassigned.
  • Heal — unassigned.
  • Hide — unassigned.
  • Intimidate — unassigned.
  • Jump — unassigned.
  • Listen — unassigned.
  • Move silently — unassigned.
  • Open lock — unassigned.
  • Perform — unassigned.
  • Profession — unassigned.
  • Ride — unassigned.
  • Search — unassigned.
  • Sense motive — unassigned.
  • Sleight of hand — unassigned.
  • Speak language — unassigned.
  • Spot — unassigned.
  • Survival — unassigned.
  • Swim — unassigned.
  • Use rope — unassigned.

Knowledge skills

Each is a separate skill, all currently unassigned for governing attribute: arcana; architecture and engineering; dungeoneering; geography; history; local; nature; nobility; religion; the planes.

skills.title: Using and Focusing Skills
skills.summary: A skill check is d20 plus the skill against a difficulty or an opposed roll. Focus tier — focused, unfocused or peripheral — caps how high the skill can be raised.
skills.summary_html: A skill check is d20 plus the skill against a difficulty or an opposed roll. Focus tier — focused, unfocused or peripheral — caps how high the skill can be raised.
skills.html:
Making a check

A skill check is the core roll: 1d20 plus the skill's level plus the bonus from its governing attribute, against a fixed difficulty or an opposed roll. Each skill has one governing attribute, listed in the The Skill List.

Focus tiers

Skills are organised into groups, and each character's groups sit at one of three tiers:

  • Focused — the character's speciality; skills here can be raised

the highest.

  • Unfocused — competent but not specialised; a lower ceiling than

focused.

  • Peripheral — everything else, with the lowest ceiling.

The tier a group sits in only limits how far its skills can be raised; it does not stop the character attempting anything. Which groups are focused and unfocused is set at Creating a Character, and the Setting Priorities rules can buy an exception for a single skill.

spell-list.title: The Spell List
spell-list.summary: The spells defined so far, each with its difficulty, school, domain and other properties.
spell-list.summary_html: The spells defined so far, each with its difficulty, school, domain and other properties.
spell-list.html:
Each spell is written with its base difficulty in brackets, then its properties. Difficulty, cost and boosting all work as How Spellcasting Works and Standard Spell Properties describe.

Cure / Cause Wounds (16)

  • Schools: life force
  • Domains: healing, or harm when reversed
  • Range: touch
  • Minimum spirit: 1

Restores hit point damage to the recipient. Cast as Cause Wounds, the same spell instead inflicts damage.

Force Bolt (2)

  • Schools: energy
  • Domains: magic
  • Range: 10, needs an attack roll
  • Damage: 4 (force)
  • Save: none
  • Minimum spirit: 0

Fires bolts of magical energy that deal force damage. Non-standard boosts:

  • Extra bolts: +4 difficulty per additional bolt.
  • Damage boost: +1 damage per bolt for each +1 difficulty.

spell-properties.title: Standard Spell Properties
spell-properties.summary: Range, duration, area and accuracy work the same across almost all spells, and can usually be boosted by casting at a higher difficulty.
spell-properties.summary_html: Range, duration, area and accuracy work the same across almost all spells, and can usually be boosted by casting at a higher difficulty.
spell-properties.html:
Most spells share these properties. Unless a spell says otherwise, each can be boosted by choosing to cast at a higher difficulty than the minimum — see How Spellcasting Works and Using a Power for what raising the difficulty costs.

Range

A spell's range is self, touch, or a number.

  • Self — the spell only ever affects the caster.
  • Touch — the caster affects themselves or another recipient by

touching them. Touching an unwilling target needs a melee attack roll.

  • A number — a range in grid squares, each square being

2 metres (roughly 2 yards). If the spell needs an attack roll to land, the listed number is short range and long range is 2 times it; use the ranged attack skill to hit. Range can be extended by 1 square per point of added difficulty.

Duration and area of effect

These are defined per spell for now; there is no general rule yet.

Accuracy

A spell's standard accuracy is 0 — no bonus or penalty to the attack roll. Accuracy increases by +1 for every point of added difficulty.

spellcasting.title: How Spellcasting Works
spellcasting.summary: Spells are powers cast with the spellcasting skill, paid for in spirit. Each spell has a school (how it is built) and a domain (what it does).
spellcasting.summary_html: Spells are powers cast with the spellcasting skill, paid for in spirit. Each spell has a school (how it is built) and a domain (what it does).
spellcasting.html:
Spells as powers

Every spell is a power. There is one casting skill — spellcasting — and one power source for all magic: spirit (see Stamina and Spirit). A spell's difficulty is used exactly as any other power's difficulty, and a margin over it reduces the spirit cost the same way.

School and domain

Every spell is tagged with both:

  • a school of magic — how the spell is constructed: life force,

energy, matter, rifts, influence and command, or illusion;

  • a domain of influence — what the spell actually does: healing,

war, trickery, love, death, nature, or magic.

A caster's access to spells, and any bonus when casting them, is described in terms of these schools and domains.

Shared properties

Beyond its own effect, every spell has a standard set of properties — range, duration, area of effect, accuracy — covered in Standard Spell Properties. The The Spell List gives the spells themselves.

using-powers.title: Using a Power
using-powers.summary: Roll the power's listed skill against its difficulty. Success costs 10 from its power source, reduced by 1 for every point the roll beat the difficulty.
using-powers.summary_html: Roll the power's listed skill against its difficulty. Success costs 10 from its power source, reduced by 1 for every point the roll beat the difficulty.
using-powers.html:
The roll

Every power lists a difficulty and the skill used to invoke it. Roll that skill (the core roll) against the difficulty. Meeting it means the power works.

The cost

A successful power costs 10 points from its power source — stamina or spirit. Every point by which the roll beat the difficulty reduces that cost by 1, so the cost is 10 + difficulty - skill_roll.

A well-practised character will eventually invoke some powers for no cost at all. A few powers set a minimum cost that this reduction cannot take you below; those say so in their own description.

The General Powers are open to every character; others come from a character's chosen area of specialisation.

weapons.title: Weapons
weapons.summary: Weapon statistics: accuracy modifier, damage rating, size, and block value. The list is incomplete.
weapons.summary_html: Weapon statistics: accuracy modifier, damage rating, size, and block value. The list is incomplete.
weapons.html:
Each weapon is listed with the statistics that feed Landing a Blow and Working Out Damage:

  • Accuracy — a modifier to the attack roll.
  • Damage — the weapon's damage rating, before the margin bonus and

before Armour reduction.

  • Size — S, M or L.
  • Block value — armour points subtracted from a blow when this

weapon is used to block.

Blank entries below are weapons that are named in the draft but not yet given numbers.

Simple melee weapons

  • Short sword — accuracy +1, damage 6, size S, block value 6.
  • Hand axe — size S; other stats not yet set.
  • Dagger — stats not yet set.
  • Staff — stats not yet set.

Martial melee weapons

  • Sword — accuracy +1, damage 8, size M.
  • Battle axe — damage 9, size M.
  • Two-handed sword — damage 12, size L.
  • Great axe — damage 12, size L.

ch-characters.title: Characters
ch-characters.summary: Attributes, the two pools of hit points, and how a starting character is built.
ch-characters.summary_html: Attributes, the two pools of hit points, and how a starting character is built.
ch-characters.html: A character is six attributes, two pools of hit points, a spread of skills, and a handful of powers. This chapter covers the first two and the process that sets all of them at the start of play.

ch-combat.title: Combat
ch-combat.summary: Landing a blow, and turning a hit into lost hit points.
ch-combat.summary_html: Landing a blow, and turning a hit into lost hit points.
ch-combat.html: Combat resolves one blow at a time. First the attacker tries to hit a defender who is either dodging or blocking; then, if the blow lands, its damage is worked out and applied.

ch-equipment.title: Equipment
ch-equipment.html: Starting gold buys weapons and armour. Both lists are partial — they carry the entries that existed when the system was first drafted, and more will be filled in.

ch-magic.title: Spells and Spellcasting
ch-magic.summary: How spells relate to powers, the properties every spell shares, and the current spell list.
ch-magic.summary_html: How spells relate to powers, the properties every spell shares, and the current spell list.
ch-magic.html: Spells are a special category of power. They use one skill, one power source, and a common framework of properties, and then each spell adds its own effect on top.

ch-overview.title: What Ico Is Trying To Do
ch-overview.summary: The design goals the rules serve, and the single mechanic they all rest on.
ch-overview.summary_html: The design goals the rules serve, and the single mechanic they all rest on.
ch-overview.html:
The Ico adventure system has a short list of goals, roughly in priority order:

  • Fun. It should be fun to play.
  • Storytelling. The rules should push the group towards descriptive

narration of the action rather than away from it.

  • Balance. Two characters built for the same power level should each

feel they contribute equally over a full adventure, and each should have something useful and non-trivial to do in most situations, and especially in combat.

  • Adventure. The standard rules are tuned to make a life of high

adventure less suicidal than the real thing would be: hit points run high relative to weapon damage, skills are impressive, powers are mighty.

  • Simplicity. Not too many dice rolls, not too much arithmetic, not

too many table lookups.

  • Realism. Reality is modelled where doing so does not break one of

the goals above.

ch-powers.title: Powers
ch-powers.summary: The two power sources, how a power is used, and the general powers any character can take.
ch-powers.summary_html: The two power sources, how a power is used, and the general powers any character can take.
ch-powers.html: Powers are the special things a character can do beyond straight skill use — extra attacks, feats of the body, and, as a special case, spells. They draw on one of two internal reserves.

ch-skills.title: Skills
ch-skills.summary: What skills are, how focus tiers cap them, and the full skill list.
ch-skills.summary_html: What skills are, how focus tiers cap them, and the full skill list.
ch-skills.html: Skills are the things a character knows how to do. A higher skill level is greater proficiency. Skills are raised with skill points, which come from character creation and from advancement.

rulebook.title: Ico Adventure System
rulebook.summary: The Ico rules, in reading order.
rulebook.summary_html: The Ico rules, in reading order.
rulebook.html:
Icosahedron: a polyhedron with twenty faces. Almost everything in this game is settled by rolling one twenty-sided die, adding what your character is good at, and seeing whether it was enough.

Read this in order the first time. After that, use the contents above — each rule stands on its own well enough to be looked up in isolation, and the in-game help shows the same text you are reading here.

This book covers character creation, skills, combat, powers, equipment and magic. The experience and progression layer — how characters advance between adventures — is being reworked and is deliberately left out for now.
